text:
Here's the whole job of a language model. It takes a sequence of tokens, and gives back a probability for every token that could come next. Not one word. A score for every token in its vocabulary, and this one has two hundred thousand. Picking one is a separate step... and how it picks is a knob you control.

To write, it picks a token, adds it to the end, and runs again on the longer input. The, cat, sat, on, the, mat, and then a token that means done. Notice what's missing from that loop: a plan. The sentence shows up because each step was reasonable, not because anything decided it in advance. There's no database, either. What it knows lives in its weights, numbers tuned in training until its guesses matched real text. That's why a well known fact and an invented citation come out of the same machinery, and sound just as sure. So what is a token, exactly?

It's a chunk of text that the vocabulary gives a single number, called its id. Sometimes a whole word, often just a piece. Take strawberry. On its own, GPT-4o's tokenizer cuts it in three: ess-tee, raw, berry. And the model gets three ids: three oh two, sixteen eighteen, nineteen seven seven two. Put a space in front, the way it sits inside a sentence, and the whole word is one id. [curious] So how many R's are in strawberry? The model never saw the letters. It has to recall facts about the spelling, instead of looking.

For English, the rule of thumb is about four characters a token, or three quarters of a word. So a thousand tokens is roughly seven hundred and fifty words. Newer tokenizers often do better. This one turns the lesson's opening, a hundred and ninety characters, into thirty-six tokens. But who decided where strawberry gets cut? Nobody did. The vocabulary was learned.
